claims.text: Introducing an intermediate-temperature dwell between rapid heating and cooling will enhance inter-element diffusion.
Dwell-enhanced diffusion will enable uniform nucleation of a single-phase solid solution.
Local composition gradients normally cause phase separation and elemental segregation in this synthesis regime.
A properly selected dwell can avoid thermal decomposition.
A properly selected dwell can avoid uncontrolled particle growth.
Rapid flash heating and cooling tends to produce mixed-phase nanoparticles.
Rapid flash heating and cooling tends to produce elemental segregation.
Rapid flash heating and cooling produces irregular morphology because diffusion is insufficient.
A sufficiently high dwell temperature will significantly enhance atomic mobility and elemental interdiffusion.
The dwell temperature must remain below thresholds for thermal decomposition and excessive coarsening.
A dwell on the order of seconds is likely long enough to permit the required diffusion.
Enhanced diffusion during the dwell will locally homogenize elements within molten or semi-molten nanoparticle droplets.
Rapid high-temperature heating of the precursors forms small liquid droplets containing multiple metals.
The very short flash-heating timeframe typically freezes compositional inhomogeneities into the final nanoparticles.
Dwell-enabled atomic redistribution overcomes kinetic barriers and stabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Nanoparticles made with the dwell will have a more uniform single-phase solid-solution structure than the rapid-heating-and-cooling baseline.
Nanoparticles made with the dwell will exhibit less elemental segregation than the baseline.
Nanoparticles made with the dwell will exhibit more controlled particle morphology than the baseline.
The rapid-heating baseline reaches approximately 2000 K.
The dwell is beneficial only within a narrow temperature window that promotes diffusion without decomposition or coarsening.
